title: Zuppa di farro
subtitle: Tuscan and Umbrian farro soup with beans and vegetables
excerpt: A hearty central Italian soup of farro (emmer wheat), borlotti beans, celery, carrot, tomato, and rosemary, simmered until the grain is swollen and tender. Thick, nutty, and deeply nourishing.
sourceNotes: Zuppa di farro is a dish of the Garfagnana (Lucca province) in Tuscany and of Umbria, where the cultivation of farro (emmer wheat) has continued since antiquity. It appears in Pellegrino Artusi's La Scienza in Cucina (1891, public domain) and in multiple Tuscan and Umbrian regional cookbooks. The Garfagnana PDO farro is specifically associated with this soup.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the soup without the final olive oil drizzle. Defrost and reheat gently, adding more stock if it has thickened.
recipe.batchNotes: Doubles well. A good batch-cook soup.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Improves the next day as the farro absorbs more liquid. Add stock when reheating.

glossaryTerms.definition: An ancient Italian wheat grain (emmer wheat, Triticum dicoccum) with a nutty flavour and chewy texture. Sold as 'whole farro' (longest cooking, needs soaking), 'semi-pearled' (slightly shorter cook), or 'pearled' (quickest). The Garfagnana and Umbrian varieties are the most prized in Italian cooking.

content.text: is the grain the Roman legions ate, and zuppa di farro is what you make when you want to understand why. The grain has a firm, nutty texture that survives long cooking without turning to mush, and it absorbs the bean-and-tomato broth around it until the soup becomes something rich, thick, and deeply satisfying. It is winter food, and it holds for several days in the fridge.

items.prepNote: semi-pearled or pearled farro; soak overnight if using whole farro

content.text: Heat the olive oil in a large, heavy saucepan over medium heat. Add the onion, celery, carrot, and garlic and cook for 10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until soft and lightly golden.
Add the tomatoes and rosemary and cook for 5 minutes, stirring. Add the stock and bring to the boil.

Add the farro and simmer until the grains are tender and the soup has thickened. Semi-pearled farro takes 35 to 40 minutes. Pearled farro takes about 25 minutes. Whole soaked farro can take up to 60 minutes.
Add the borlotti beans for the last 10 minutes. Remove the rosemary sprigs. Taste and season. Serve in deep bowls with a drizzle of good extra-virgin olive oil and black pepper.

items.symptom: Farro is still tough after 40 minutes
items.cause: Whole farro was not soaked, or heat too low
items.fix: Whole farro needs an overnight soak. Always check the packet. Semi-pearled should be tender at 40 minutes at a steady simmer.

content.text: Zuppa di farro is the signature soup of the Garfagnana and the Lunigiana, the mountain territories north of Lucca, and of Umbria. Farro has been cultivated in these areas without interruption since antiquity. They are poor, remote regions where the grain survived long after it was replaced by wheat elsewhere in Italy. Farro soup is their most characteristic dish. Garfagnana farro has its own PDO designation. In the restaurant cooking of Tuscany and Umbria, the soup is treated as a dish of cultural importance. It appears on menus in Lucca, Perugia, and Spoleto alongside far more technically complex dishes.
